questions.q: Which of these is a real reason Linux endpoint protection historically lagged behind Windows tooling?
options: Distro diversity (different kernels, package managers, and init systems) makes a single agent harder to build and support
Linux computers are physically incapable of running antivirus software
Linux has never been targeted by any malware of any kind
Signature-based scanning is technically impossible on Linux
questions.explain: Along with historically lower perceived risk and a server/container-heavy deployment pattern, distro fragmentation genuinely made building one broadly-compatible agent harder.

options: An open-source, signature-based antivirus engine for Linux, run with commands like clamscan and freshclam
A commercial behavioral EDR platform exclusive to Windows
A Linux kernel module that replaces the need for any other security tool
A network firewall configuration tool
questions.explain: ClamAV is the traditional open-source signature scanner for Linux. clamscan runs an on-demand scan; freshclam updates the signature database.

questions.q: Which vendors now ship real commercial EDR agents with Linux support, not just Windows ones?
options: CrowdStrike Falcon, SentinelOne, and Microsoft Defender for Endpoint
No commercial EDR vendor has ever supported Linux
Only ClamAV's publisher offers any Linux security product
Linux support is exclusive to Microsoft Defender Antivirus, not Defender for Endpoint
questions.explain: CrowdStrike Falcon, SentinelOne, and Microsoft Defender for Endpoint all provide Linux sensors with the same behavioral monitoring and response capability as their Windows agents.

questions.q: What does auditd provide to a Linux EDR agent?
options: Kernel-level logging of system calls and process/file events, used as a telemetry source
A graphical dashboard for configuring firewall rules
A replacement for the Linux kernel itself
Automatic patching of installed packages
questions.explain: auditd, the Linux Audit Framework, logs syscalls and process/file events at the kernel level, giving agents the behavioral visibility ETW provides on Windows.

questions.q: Why do modern Linux security agents increasingly use eBPF instead of relying only on auditd?
options: eBPF lets an agent hook low-level kernel events with less performance overhead than older audit mechanisms
eBPF makes signature-based scanning completely unnecessary
auditd was removed from the Linux kernel and no longer exists
eBPF only works for scanning files, not monitoring behavior
questions.explain: eBPF is a kernel technology that provides low-level visibility with lower overhead than traditional audit mechanisms, which matters on busy production servers.
